feed_card.headline: Silica aerogel is up to 99.8% air, yet a piece weighing 2 grams can hold up a 2.5-kilogram brick.
teasers: It was invented to settle a bet
It brought comet dust back to Earth
Cool to the touch over an open flame

sections.content: Silica aerogel is up to 99.8% air, yet a piece weighing 2 grams can hold up a 2.5-kilogram brick.

sections.content: Start with the density. The lightest silica aerogel weighs about 3 milligrams per cubic centimetre. Water weighs 1,000, and even the air in the room comes in near 1.2. So the material is only a few times heavier than air, and to the eye it is a faint blue haze you can see straight through. Here is the part that does not follow. That same wisp is stiff enough to bridge a gap and carry a brick, and it blocks heat so well that a flame held underneath barely warms the top. So little material should be fragile and should leak heat, yet it does neither.

items: Two grams of aerogel, roughly the weight of two paperclips, will hold a 2.5-kilogram brick placed on top.
The load rides on a lattice of silica strands only a few nanometres across, most of the block being the empty space between them.

content.body: In 1931 Samuel Stephens Kistler, a chemist at the College of the Pacific in California, set out to win an argument. He and a colleague, Charles Learned, had wagered over whether the liquid inside a jelly could be swapped for gas while the jelly kept its shape. Dry a jelly the ordinary way and it shrinks to a hard nub, the liquid dragging the walls inward on its way out. Kistler pushed the liquid past its critical point instead, into a state that is neither liquid nor gas and has no surface tension to do the dragging, then bled it off. It worked. What remained held its full volume, a solid that was almost all air. He named it aerogel and published it in Nature the same year.

key_figures.name: Samuel Stephens Kistler
key_figures.one_line: In 1931 he replaced a gel's liquid with gas without collapsing it, and named the near-weightless result aerogel.

content.title: Heat can barely find a way across it
content.body: The same emptiness that makes aerogel light makes it a superb insulator. Heat crosses a solid by rattling from atom to atom, and aerogel is mostly the space between atoms, threaded by a thin silica web with little to rattle through. Its pores are so small that even the trapped air struggles to carry heat, since a gas molecule hits a pore wall before it hits another molecule. NASA measured a silica aerogel at about 39 times the insulating power of the best fiberglass. Hold a flame beneath a thin slab and the top stays cool enough to touch.
content.image_caption: Matches rest unlit on a slab of aerogel held over a flame; the heat barely reaches them.

content.title: It caught comet dust at 6 kilometres a second without burning it
content.body: In 2004 NASA's Stardust probe swept through the coma of comet Wild 2 carrying a rack of aerogel tiles. Grains of comet dust struck at about 6 kilometres a second, fast enough to melt or vaporize on any ordinary surface. The aerogel let them bury themselves instead, braking each grain gently along a slender carrot-shaped track. The capsule parachuted into the Utah desert in 2006 with more than 10,000 captured particles, the first pieces of a comet ever brought to Earth.

content.title: The lightest-solid crown has moved to carbon
content.body: For decades aerogel was the lightest solid anyone had made, and in 2002 a NASA silica aerogel at 3 milligrams per cubic centimetre went into Guinness World Records as the least dense solid. It does not hold that title now. Aerographite took it in 2012, then a graphene aerogel in 2013 at 0.16 milligrams per cubic centimetre, lighter than air itself. Silica aerogel is still the version made by the sheet and bonded into insulating blankets, so the workhorse and the record holder are now different materials.

sections.content: Kistler's real result was a proof that a solid does not have to be mostly solid. Take away nearly all the mass, leave a scaffold a few nanometres thick, and the shape and stiffness survive while new properties appear. That idea outgrew silica. Aerogels now come in carbon, metal oxides, and cellulose, and they insulate pipelines and jackets, shield spacecraft, and soak up oil spills. Often the useful part of a solid is the emptiness built into it.

content.question: How can aerogel be almost all air and still be a rigid solid?
options: It is a continuous solid network whose volume is nearly all empty pores
It is a dense metal foam that only looks light
It is a gas frozen in place by extreme cold
It traps helium, which weighs almost nothing
content.explanation: The silica forms an unbroken, spidery skeleton that threads through the whole block. There is very little of it, but because it is connected it holds a shape and bears a load.

content.question: Aerogel is such a good insulator mainly because...
options: the silica reflects heat away like a mirror
it is always kept under a vacuum
it converts the heat into light
its pores are so tiny that the trapped air can barely conduct heat
content.explanation: There is little solid to carry heat, and the pores are smaller than the distance an air molecule normally travels, so even the trapped gas conducts poorly.

content.question: In the standard demonstration, how much can a 2-gram piece of aerogel support?
options: About twice its own weight
About fifty times its own weight
About 1,250 times its own weight, a 2.5-kilogram brick
Effectively unlimited weight
content.explanation: Pushed straight down, the thin silica network is remarkably strong, so a 2-gram sample holds a 2.5-kilogram brick, over a thousand times its own weight.

content.question: Why did NASA use aerogel to catch comet dust on the Stardust mission?
options: It is magnetic and pulls dust toward it
It let fast grains slow down gradually instead of vaporizing on impact
It is sticky and traps particles like glue
It is transparent, so particles were easy to spot
content.explanation: Grains arriving at about 6 kilometres a second would burn up on a solid surface. Sinking into the aerogel, each one brakes along a long track and survives largely intact.

content.question: Is silica aerogel still the least dense solid known?
options: Yes, nothing has ever been made lighter
Yes, but only when measured in a vacuum
No, it was never especially light to begin with
No, a graphene aerogel is now far lighter, near 0.16 mg per cubic centimetre
content.explanation: Silica aerogel held the record for decades. Carbon versions passed it, aerographite in 2012 and a graphene aerogel in 2013, the latter lighter than air itself.

content.question: What broader point did Kistler's invention establish about solids?
options: That any solid can be turned into a gas
That lighter materials are always weaker
That a solid can be almost all empty space and still keep its shape and stiffness
That air is technically a kind of solid
content.explanation: Aerogel showed that stripping out nearly all the mass, leaving only a fine scaffold, can preserve a solid's structure while adding new properties like extreme insulation.

content.myth: Aerogel is called frozen smoke because it is made from smoke.
content.reality: There is no smoke in it. The bluish, ghostly look comes from its fine structure scattering blue light, the same reason the sky is blue.

content.myth: If it can hold up a brick, it must be tough to handle.
content.reality: It is strong pushing straight down but brittle everywhere else. Poke or bend a pure block and it cracks like dry meringue, which is why most of it ships bonded into flexible blankets.

content.myth: It feels cold or damp, like a gel.
content.reality: It feels like firm, dry foam at room temperature. The gel is only a stage in making it; once the liquid is gone, what is left is a dry solid that is mostly air.
